**A. FACT / EVIDENCE.** Negm, verbatim: observations comprise "**changes in leakage rate** after introducing a new PRV setting and the full list of PRV and VSP settings"; "the observation space describes the **nodal leakage rate** and actuator settings". Negm's own caveats: "this study depends on clean data … requires sensor data across the network" and "well-developed DRL models are very sensitive to incorrect observation data which could wrongly trigger destructive valve actions". Belfadil, verbatim: "at each time step, the agent receives the **pressure at demand nodes, tank levels, and time**; this is the state `s` of the environment." Hu MARL eq. Mosetlhe: "the critical node is defined as the sensitive node with the lowest pressure"; control from critical-node pressure is established (Berardi 2015; Page 2017c). Olmuştur & Uysal 2025: "although maintaining constant pressure at a single critical point appears effective, it does not necessarily guarantee optimal pressure distribution across the whole system; therefore network-level modelling is essential."

**B. Feature-by-feature audit** (the six questions applied):

| Feature | Physically observable? | Available at decision time? | Leaks future info? | Shortcut risk? | Real-world available? | Supports RQ? | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pressure at instrumented nodes | ✅ SCADA | ✅ | No | Low | ✅ | ✅ core | **INCLUDE** |
| Pressure at **all** nodes | ❌ | ✅ | No | **High** (uses unavailable information) | ❌ | Partly | **EXCLUDE** |
| Flow at metered sections | ✅ DMA inlet meters | ✅ | No | Low | ✅ | ✅ | **INCLUDE** |
| Tank level | ✅ | ✅ | No | Low | ✅ | ✅ closes pump coupling | **INCLUDE** |
| Actuator state (current setting) | ✅ | ✅ | No | Low | ✅ | ✅ | **INCLUDE** |
| Previous action `a_{t-1}` | ✅ | ✅ | No | Low | ✅ | ✅ **required for the smoothness term** | **INCLUDE** |
| Time encoding `sin/cos(2πt/24)` | ✅ | ✅ | No | 🔶 **Yes — schedule memorisation** | ✅ | Ambiguous | **INCLUDE + test (F3)** |
| **Nodal leakage rate** | ❌ **a model quantity, not a measurement** | Only in simulation | No | **Critical** | ❌ **does not exist** | Would inflate performance | **PROHIBIT** (oracle run only) |
| Total network leakage | 🔶 only via balance/MNF, with lag | Lagged | No | Medium | Partly | Partly | **EXCLUDE from main** |
| **True demand multiplier** | ❌ | ✅ in simulation | **YES — future information** | **Critical** | ❌ | **Destroys sub-question 1** | **PROHIBIT** |
| Recent history window (`H` steps) | ✅ | ✅ | No | Low | ✅ | Partly (POMDP aid) | **OPTIONAL** (LSTM alternative) |

**C. Two information-leakage traps, stated precisely.** (1) **True demand multiplier in the observation ⇒ leakage of future information.** If the agent sees the actual consumption multiplier for the current step, the uncertainty problem dissolves and sub-question 1 becomes vacuous. Permitted: the *effect* of demand (observed pressures, observed flows). Prohibited: the multiplier itself. (2) **Time encoding is double-edged.** With it, the agent can maintain an hourly lookup table instead of reacting to state — degenerating into a learned TMPC rather than adaptive control, which directly undercuts the Proposal's central claim. Remedy: keep it, but ablate it (A9) **and** run the pattern-break test (out-of-phase peak). If performance collapses, the policy was time-driven.

**D. Options.** **S1 minimal** `[p^CN, h^tank, a_{t-1}]` — lowest dimension, most operational, comparable to industrial CLPC; but a single node does not represent network pressure distribution (Olmuştur & Uysal), so violations elsewhere may go unseen. **S2 balanced** `[p^M, q^F, h^tank, a_{t-1}, φ(t)]` — every component SCADA-measurable, controlled dimension, deployable, network coverage; the choice of `M` is itself a design decision needing documentation and sensitivity. **S3 rich** — adds all-node pressures, all pipe flows, nodal `Q^leak`, history; higher ceiling and valuable as an **oracle upper bound**, but **not deployable** and prone to sample-inefficiency and overfitting.

**Recommendation:** S2 as the main design; S3 restricted to a **single** oracle run; S1 in ablation A8. The S2↔S3 gap quantifies the **cost of observability** — a quantity neither Negm nor Belfadil measured, and a genuine (if modest) contribution. Normalisation statistics computed from **training scenarios only**, stored and published. **Validation:** the pattern-break test; an audit that no feature exposes a future value; permutation importance to detect shortcut reliance. **DECISION: NOT LOCKED — READY TO LOCK (F1/F2/F3/F4).**

## 12. Action Decision Analysis

**A. FACT / EVIDENCE.** Hu MARL, verbatim: "The action of the **pressure reducing valve (PRV)** agent was to set the **outlet pressure**, and its action space was determined based on the minimum pressure requirement of consumers and the valve inlet pressure. The valve inlet pressure of the PRV was calculated using **1,000 random interaction episodes** with the environment, and the maximum valve inlet pressure was set as the upper limit of the action space of the PRV agent." And: "The pump was modelled as a **variable-speed pump with a speed range of 0.7–1** considering mechanical constraints." Negm: action-space bounds "0 to 70 for valves and **unlimited speed for pumps**". **Dai, Kim & Kim 2016 / Dai 2021, verbatim:** "PRV models used so far for pressure regulation are **two-state models** that cannot describe many situations occurring in WDS. In this paper we extend the existing model with a **three-state** model for the PRV … able to explain the three operating states of the PRV (**open, normal, check valve**)." Negm §7.2, verbatim: "it was assumed that pressure valves are able to process precise settings provided by the agent whereas in practice **some control errors can be expected**." Negm: "most water utilities change PRV settings **daily**." Proposal assumption: "فضای عمل پیوسته برای تنظیم **تدریجی** تجهیزات".

**B. INFERENCE — the physical problem no DRL work in the corpus models.** When the agent commands an outlet-pressure setpoint, the PRV honours it **only in the normal state**. If the setpoint exceeds available upstream head the valve goes **fully open** and the command is not realised; under reverse flow it becomes a **check valve**. Therefore **commanded action ≠ realised action**, part of the action space is effectively inert, and the reward signal contains plateau regions that slow learning and mislead interpretation. Also: Negm's "unlimited pump speed" is physically invalid; Hu's `[0.7, 1.0]` mechanical bound is scientifically better.

**C. PRV specifics.** *Setpoint interpretation:* target outlet head in metres. *Valid range:* `[p^min_service, s̄_

v]`, with `s̄_v` derived empirically from **1,000 random rollouts** (Hu's documented method — an empirical bound, not a guess). *Operational-state behaviour:* three states per Dai; only the normal state realises the command.

**D. VSP specifics.** Speed ratio `ω ∈ [0.7, 1.0]`, a mechanical constraint taken verbatim from Hu. Below 0.7 the pump is not a defensible operating point; above 1.0 exceeds nominal speed. Negm's "unlimited" is rejected on physical grounds.

**E. Options.**

| | A: absolute | B: incremental | **C: absolute + rate-limit projection** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Formulation | `a_t = [s^PRV_v, ω_u]` directly | `s_t = clip(s_{t-1} + Δ_t, …)` | `s_t = clip(s̃_t, s_{t-1} ± δ)` |
| Cumulative drift | None | Possible | None |
| Markovianity | Better | Requires `s_{t-1}` in state (present in S2) | Better |
| Physical feasibility between steps | ❌ large jumps possible | ✅ structural | ✅ **hard guarantee** |
| Comparability with optimiser baselines | ✅ they emit settings directly | ❌ complicated | ✅ |
| Corpus precedent | Negm, Belfadil, Hu, Mosetlhe — **all absolute** | **None** | — |
| Smoothness handling | Penalty only | Structural | Structural **plus** penalty |
| New parameter | — | `δ` | `δ` ⇒ sensitivity S8 |
| Risk | Medium | Medium | **Low** |

**F. Action Realization Rate — definition and validation.** *Definition:* at every step the **realised** setting is read back from EPANET after the hydraulic solve; `ARR = (steps in which the commanded setpoint was actually realised) / (total steps)`, reported per actuator and aggregated. *Validation:* construct a scenario with a setpoint deliberately above available upstream head — ARR **must** drop measurably; if it does not, the read-back is wrong, not the physics. *Why it matters:* it is the cheapest methodological contribution available (one logged quantity), it has no precedent in the corpus, it directly tests operational executability, and it diagnoses the reward plateaus that the three-state PRV behaviour creates.

**Recommendation:** Option C. `s^PRV_{v,t} = clip(s̃_{v,t}, s^PRV_{v,t-1} ± δ_v)` and `ω_{u,t} = clip(ω̃_{u,t}, ω_{u,t-1} ± δ_u)`, with `s^PRV_v ∈ [p^min_service, s̄_v]` and `ω_u ∈ [0.7, 1.0]`; policy outputs `tanh`, rescaled to the physical range, so structurally invalid actions are impossible. `δ` at 10 % of range as reference, `{5 %, 10 %, 20 %}` in sensitivity S8. Pure incremental in ablation A11. ARR logged and reported. **Do not assume a mathematically valid action is physically executable — ARR is the instrument that enforces this.** **DECISION: NOT LOCKED — READY TO LOCK (G1/G2/G3).**

## 13. Reward Decision Analysis

**A. FACT / EVIDENCE.** Negm eq. 4-3: `R = Σ_j[(v_after − v_before)·scale₁ + ((Q_lb − Q_la)/Q_lb)·scale₂]`, with `v ∈ {0,1}` indicating whether node pressure is below 10 m or above 70 m. Negm §4.2.4: ratio **6:1** best for leakage, **1:5** best for violations, **3:1** best overall; and "the two extremes of the ratios do not necessarily produce the best result for the corresponding objective". Negm Table 5-4 + p. 130: PPO reached 73.4 % leakage with **304 violations** and "**exploited the leakage objective at the expense of the pressure violation objective**". Ledesma 2020 and 2024: the four canonical WDN control objectives are economic, safety, **smoothness**, water quality. Ma et al. 2024: frequent pump switching caused "**wear of pump units**"; the proposed scheme "keeps the number of pumps relatively stable". Olmuştur & Uysal 2025: PID on PRVs is prone to "instability or oscillation". Hu MARL: "**water loss dominates the scheduling process**, and the scheduling solutions … are mainly affected by the **demand pattern** rather than the **energy tariff**"; pump efficiency "**simplified to 0.75**"; eq. (17) `H_tank,fin ≥ H_tank,ini` as a hard constraint.

**B. INFERENCE — two structural defects in Negm's form, plus one omission.**

| Defect | Analysis | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| **W1: binary violation term** | `v ∈ {0,1}` ⇒ zero gradient between 9.9 m and 2 m. The agent is **indifferent** between a marginal violation and a catastrophic outage | Continuous severity `ν_{j,t}` in **metres** ⇒ meaningful gradient at every level |
| **W2: per-node normalisation** | `(Q_lb − Q_la)/Q_lb` gives a node with negligible baseline leakage the same weight as a node with enormous leakage ⇒ the agent is incentivised to work on unimportant nodes | Normalise by **total network leakage** in the reference scenario |
| **W3: only two terms** | Negm has leakage + violation. The Proposal requires four objectives: leakage, pressure, **smoothness**, **energy** | Terms three and four designed from the outset with literature backing (Ledesma, Ma) |

**C. The reward-hacking evidence, and the confound.** *Direct evidence:* PPO with Negm's reward achieved the best leakage and the worst violations, in Negm's own words "exploited". *New inference this phase (Medium-High):* Table 5-4 partitions cleanly — the ~65 %/46–78-violation cluster is exactly the **tuned** agents plus the classical optimisers, and the ~73 %/264–304 cluster is exactly the **untuned** on-policy agents; Negm states "**All untuned** DRL algorithms performed less favourably". So the hacking magnitude is entangled with **(a)** the binary violation term, **(b)** absent tuning, **(c)** the 20 k budget. **Consequence: the project cannot claim its reward redesign fixed the behaviour unless A6 runs at equal tuning and equal budget.** This is why A6 is promoted to Tier 1 and why the contribution wording in N1/A3 must stay conservative.

**D. Failure modes F1–F11 — resolution ownership.**

| # | Failure mode | Resolved by | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| **F1** | Faking leakage reduction via supply curtailment | **Simulator choice** (PDA) + evaluation (DSR as an independent primary metric) | ✅ Resolved |
| **F2** | Indifference to violation severity | **Reward design** (continuous `ν` in metres, `β=2`) + evaluation (max violation, P95) | ✅ Resolved |
| **F3** | Weight choice silently favouring leakage | **Evaluation** (full Pareto front) + feasibility-first rule | ✅ Resolved |
| **F4** | Per-node normalisation distortion | **Reward design** (global normalisation by `L^ref`) | ✅ Resolved |
| **F5** | Focusing only on night hours (highest leakage) | **Evaluation** (hour-resolved reporting) — Negm found a 3–6 am vulnerability | ✅ Resolved |
| **F6** | Excessive conservatism (high `w_V` ⇒ high pressure, high leakage) | **Evaluation** (both metrics always reported; comparison against the fixed-pressure baseline, which must not be beaten in the wrong direction) + test T10 | ✅ Resolved |

| | **A: weighted multi-objective (revised)** | B: constrained / Lagrangian | C: safety filter |
|---|---|---|---|
| Covers the Proposal's 4 objectives | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Pressure constraint tradeable? | ❌ **yes — the weakness** | ✅ no | ✅ no (run-time) |

**Recommended form:**

`r_t = −[ w_L·L̃_t + w_V·Ṽ_t + w_S·S̃_t + w_E·Ẽ_t ]`, all terms dimensionless and pre-normalised against a reference scenario:

`L̃_t = Σ_j Q^leak_{j,t} / L^ref_step` · `Ṽ_t = (1/|J|) Σ_j (ν_{j,t}/ν^scale)^β` with `ν_{j,t} = max(0, p^min − p_{j,t}) + max(0, p_{j,t} − p^max)` **in metres** · `S̃_t = (1/(|V|+|U|))[ Σ_v (|Δs_{v,t}|/δ_v)² + Σ_u (|Δω_{u,t}|/δ_u)² ]` · `Ẽ_t = P^pump_t Δt / E^ref_step` with `η = 0.75` and **no tariff modelling** · plus the hard constraint `H_tank,fin ≥ H_tank,ini`.

Weight selection: sweep `w_V/w_L ∈ {1/7, 1/5, 1/3, 1, 3, 5, 7}` at identical budget and seeds, report the **entire** Pareto front, select by feasibility-first. **Final weights are NOT chosen here and must not be — that is an explicit researcher decision after the front exists.**

## 14. Reward Validation — battery T1–T10

The reward must be validated **on synthetic inputs, before any training**, so that training results are interpretable. Each test constructs a controlled state transition and checks the sign and magnitude of the reward.

| # | Scenario | Expected reward direction | Status | Questionable assumption? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **T1** | Leakage falls, all pressures in range | **Increase** | **MANDATORY** — sanity floor | None |
| **T2** | Leakage constant, one node drops to 5 m | **Decrease**, appreciably | **MANDATORY** | None |
| **T3** | Leakage −10 %, but one node violates by 3 m | **Must decrease** (feasibility-first). If it increases, the weights are wrong | **MANDATORY — decisive** | ⚠️ Depends on the chosen `w_V/w_L`; the test defines what "wrong" means only *after* a weight is picked, so it must be re-run for every swept weight |
| **T4** | Peak demand, multiplier ×1.5 | Must not become artificially generous; normalisation should absorb the scale | **MANDATORY** | ⚠️ Assumes `L^ref` is scale-appropriate; if the reference scenario is itself a peak scenario the test is weak |
| **T5** | Night, multiplier ×0.4, high pressure | Should signal the leakage-reduction opportunity | RECOMMENDED | None |
| **T6** | All nodes at `p^max` | The violation term must activate (upper bound, not only lower) | **MANDATORY** | None — this specifically catches a one-sided violation implementation |
| **T7** | One PRV closed as far as possible | **DSR must fall and reward must go negative.** If not, PDA is not working | **MANDATORY — decisive** | None. This is the strongest single check that the PDA/emitter separation is real |
| **T8** | `ω = 0.7` forced at peak | Reward must register the violation caused by the pressure drop | RECOMMENDED | None |
| **T9** | Compute `L̃, Ṽ, S̃, Ẽ` in the reference scenario | All must be `O(1)`; if one is ~10³ larger, normalisation is broken | **MANDATORY** | None. This is the guard against the `β=2`/`ν^scale` miscalibration risk in H1 |
| **T10** | Reward of the fixed-pressure baseline policy | Yields a reference number; any learned policy must beat it or training failed | **MANDATORY** | None |

**Mandatory: T1, T2, T3, T4, T6, T7, T9, T10. Optional: T5, T8.** **Hard gate: T3 and T7 must pass before any training run.** If T7 fails, every downstream result is invalid because the PDA mechanism is inert.

**Methodological note.** This battery does automatically, before training, what Negm did visually after training via five render functions ("the render function … can help in diagnosing any problem in the agent behaviour. It can also help in fine-tuning the reward function"). Automated pre-training tests are cheaper and repeatable.

## 15. Demand Uncertainty Decision Analysis

**A. FACT / EVIDENCE.** Hu E-PPO, verbatim: two-step randomisation "to mimic the **time and space** effects" — hourly random multipliers on the default pattern, then nodal random multipliers on base demand; "Both random multipliers of time and space follow the **truncated normal distribution** … restricted to a certain range of values, such as **(1 − Δ, 1 + Δ)**"; "The **initial water levels of the tanks follow a uniform distribution of (0, 1)**"; large consumers — "… compared to the general consumer and **do not apply a randomisation method to it**". Hu MARL: multipliers "follow a truncated normal distribution with a range from **0.7 to 1.3**" (Δ = 0.3); "All the test cases are randomly generated from **the same distribution as the training cases**." Hu E-PPO evaluation: "**100 random test cases** from the same distribution as the training cases", plus "**15 optimisation test cases** under three different demand distributions". Hu E-PPO, verbatim: "when the environment has **great uncertainty**, it is **difficult to learn an optimal strategy** network, as the state transition becomes blurred. The selection of the agent tends to be **conservative**." Proposal: only "شرایط مصرف عادی، ساعات اوج مصرف و شرایط کم‌مصرف"; and the Proposal itself criticises prior work for examining performance "در شرایط نسبتاً ثابت و الگوهای مصرف از پیش تعیین‌شده".

**B. INFERENCE.** The Proposal's three named scenarios are **deterministic scenarios, not uncertainty** — they are precisely the deficiency the Proposal attributes to prior work. Hu's protocol has three properties the Proposal lacks: uncertainty that is **both spatial and temporal**, a **parametric and reproducible** distribution, and a **physical refinement** (large consumers carry lower uncertainty). And because **both** Hu papers tested in-distribution only, holding out a Δ level is a genuine advance rather than a replication.

**C. Options.**

| | A: scalar perturbation | **B: Hu-style stochastic** | C: historical profiles | D: Monte Carlo | **E: distribution shift** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Definition | One multiplier × base pattern | Spatial-temporal truncated normal, Δ parametric | Real SCADA data | Mass sampling | Test on unseen Δ or pattern shape |
| Realism | Low | **High** | Highest | High | High |
| Reproducibility | Highest | **High** (seed + parameter) | **Low** (proprietary) | High | High |
| Difficulty | Negligible | Low | High (data access) | Medium | Low |
| Generalisation value | **Low** | High | High | High | **Highest** |
| Coverage | One-dimensional | Demand space | Limited history | Wide | Out-of-distribution |
| Cost | Negligible | Low | Low after data | **High** | Low |
| Evidence | Mosetlhe (120 % demand test) | **Hu ×2** | — (absent from corpus) | — | Negm (random bursts) |
| Verdict | **OPTIONAL** (cheap stress test) | **MANDATORY** | **SCOPE-EXPANDING → exclude** | **OPTIONAL → exclude on cost** | **MANDATORY** |

**D. Train / validation / test separation — engineered, not assumed.**

| Dimension | Train | Validation (weight & checkpoint selection) | Test (once, at the end) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Seed stream | `{1..S_tr}` | `{S_tr+1..}` | **Separate and locked until the end** |
| `Δ` | `{0.3, 0.6}` | same | same (in-distribution) **+ `Δ = 0.9` held out (OOD)** |
| Daily pattern shape | Net3 reference | same | same **+ out-of-phase pattern (OOD #2)** |
| Initial tank level | `U(0,1)` | `U(0,1)` | `U(0,1)` with a separate seed |
| Normalisation statistics | computed from **train only** | applied | applied, never recomputed |
| Episode count | — | ≥50 | **≥100 per seed** |

**Hard rules:** reward-weight and checkpoint selection **only** on validation, never on test; the test set runs **once**, at the end; if the design changes after seeing test results, a **new** test set must be constructed and the change reported explicitly.

**Risk requiring a Step-2 check:** if `Δ = 0.9` is so severe that even the best baseline violates constraints, the performance ceiling is artificial. **Check in Step 2; if so, reduce the OOD Δ to ≈0.75 and report the adjustment.**

**Recommendation:** B mandatory as generator + E mandatory as the evaluation layer + A optional as a cheap stress test + C excluded (scope) + D excluded (cost). **DECISION: NOT LOCKED — READY TO LOCK (K1/K2/K3/K4).**

## 16. Baseline Decision Analysis

**A. FACT / EVIDENCE.** Seminar lists FOPC (fixed outlet pressure control) and **TMPC** (time-modulated) among pressure-management strategies, and reports Vicente et al. 2016 calling fixed-outlet control effectively obsolete while remaining the industrial reference — **and Vicente et al. 2016 is now fully identified** (§7.1). Proposal: "مقایسه… با کنترل ثابت شیرهای فشارشکن". Negm: "most water utilities change PRV settings **daily**" ⇒ TMPC is industry practice, not a straw man. **Negm Table 5-4 (decisive): DE achieved the best average reward (995.2) and the fewest violations (46) — better than all eight DRL agents.** Hu: "GA converges after 100 epochs … therefore, the results of GA are considered as **optimal solutions and benchmarks**". Mosetlhe: classical P/PID control from one measured point is standard practice. Olmuştur & Uysal 2025: "one of the most widely used methods for real-time PRV adjustment is the PID controller", with **19 % loss reduction and 41 % fewer failures in a real field deployment**. Seminar on MPC: "دقت عملکرد آن **کاملاً به صحت مدل ریاضی وابسته** است". Proposal sub-question 2 ⇒ a single-objective control is required. Kåge 2025: "only a few studies have benchmarked policy-based against value-based RL algorithms".

**B. INFERENCE — the fairness question is where a comparison is won or lost.** Two structural asymmetries: DRL trains once then infers in 0.42 s, whereas metaheuristics must solve **each case separately** at 1181–1699 s (Hu Table 3). And **regime dependence:** Negm ch. 5 (background leakage, quasi-static) had metaheuristics beating DRL, while ch. 6 (random bursts, dynamic) had DRL winning. **Therefore the test regime determines the answer.** If the thesis tests only quasi-static scenarios it will likely report DRL losing; if only dynamic, winning. **The honest design tests both regimes and reports the dependence as a finding.**

**C. Classification.**

| Baseline | Class | What it isolates | Fairness requirements |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Fixed-outlet PRV** | **MANDATORY** | Absolute reference — without it no number means anything | Tuned by an **explicit industrial criterion**: the lowest setting satisfying `p^min` at peak hour. **Not arbitrary** — an arbitrary setting manufactures a weak baseline |
| **TMPC** | **MANDATORY** | **Is the advantage from learning, or merely from changing settings hourly?** The single most important baseline for innovation 1 | Same network, same test scenarios, same leakage model, same PDA |
| **DE** | **MANDATORY** | Performance ceiling — how far from optimal are we? | **Hydraulic-evaluation budget documented and increased to plateau.** Giving DE 50 evaluations when it needs 5,000 builds a straw baseline |
| **Single-objective (leakage-only) PPO** | **MANDATORY** | Direct control for sub-question 2 | Identical budget, seeds, test set |
| **SAC** | **MANDATORY** (Phase 2 said "recommended"; promoted — internal validity requires it) | Is the advantage from PPO or from the environment/reward? | **Equal timestep budget, equal seed count, equal tuning trials** |
| **P / PID on the critical node** | **RECOMMENDED** | Is RL needed at all, or does simple feedback suffice? Strong field evidence (Olmuştur & Uysal) | Same network and test set |
| **GA** | **RECOMMENDED** | Most conventional in both international and Persian PM literature; Hu's optimal reference | Documented evaluation budget |
| **PSO** | **OPTIONAL** | Metaheuristic diversity; weaker than DE in both Negm and Hu | — |
| **Nelder-Mead** | **OPTIONAL** | Cheap local-optimisation reference | — |
| **MPC** | **REJECTED** | High cost, marginal value in this scope; a P-controller answers the same question far cheaper | — |
| **MADDPG** | **REJECTED** | Scope change; approved algorithm is PPO | — |

**Uniform fairness protocol across all baselines:** same network, same demand scenarios (same seeds), same simulator, same leakage model, same PDA parameters, same constraints, same locked test set. Report the four cost quantities separately (§4.5 M3) plus the **break-even ≈ 4 operational cases**.

**Pre-accepted risk:** DE may beat PPO in the quasi-static regime. **This must be reported honestly and interpreted as regime dependence — a finding, not a failure.** **Do not confuse "lower leakage" with "better system performance", and do not confuse "PPO is chosen" with "PPO is proven superior".**

**DECISION: NOT LOCKED — READY TO LOCK (M1/M2/M3).**

## 17. Evaluation Decision Analysis

**Governing rule, derived from evidence rather than caution:** Negm Table 5-4 shows any leakage figure can be bought by paying in violations. **Therefore every leakage report must carry violations and DSR in the same row of the same table.**

**Primary metrics (decisive in ranking).**

| Metric | Formula | Construct measured | Why needed | Gameable? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Leakage volume** | `L = Σ_t Δt Σ_j k_j p_{j,t}^{N₁}` | The core objective, m³/day; reported **absolute and relative to the fixed baseline** | The thesis subject | **Yes — via service curtailment**, hence never reported alone |
| **Violation volume** | `VV = Σ_t Σ_j ν_{j,t} Δt` (metre·hours) | Total constraint-breach severity | Captures severity, unlike a count | Hard to game; insensitive to distribution |
| **Violation count** | `#{(j,t) : ν_{j,t} > 0}` | Breach frequency | **Comparability with Negm**, who reported exactly this (PPO 304, DE 46) | **Yes — by trading many small for few large**, hence paired with max violation |
| **Maximum violation** | `max_{j,t} ν_{j,t}` | Worst-case safety | An 8 m breach is unacceptable even with a good mean | **No** — cannot be averaged away |
| **DSR** | `Σ_{t,j} d_{j,t} / Σ_{t,j} D_{j,t}` | Service adequacy | **The only detector of failure mode F1.** Meaningful only under PDA | No |

**Secondary metrics.** Mean network pressure `p̄` (context, not ranked). Pressure variability `sd_t(p̄_t)` or `max_t p̄_t − min_t p̄_t` — **operationalises the Proposal's otherwise undefined "pressure stability"**. Pump energy `E = Σ_t P^pump_t Δt` (kWh). Actuator movement `Σ_t Σ_v |Δs_{v,t}| + Σ_t Σ_u |Δω_{u,t}|`. Tank recovery `|h^tank_T − h^tank_0|` (enforces F7; evidence-backed via Hu eq. 17). **ARR** (operational validity). Inference time per decision step (Proposal objective 3). Training time (reported separately, once).

**Learning diagnostics.** Episodic return; value loss; policy loss; entropy (detects policy collapse); explained variance; clip fraction and approx-KL (PPO-specific health); **learning curves as mean ± SD across seeds** — reported so a reader can see whether each algorithm converged or merely ran out of budget.

**Ranking rule — pre-registration mandatory (N2).** `max violation > safety threshold` ⇒ **FAIL**, unranked · `DSR < 0.99` ⇒ **FAIL** · among feasible policies rank by leakage `L` · on statistical ties, by energy, then actuator movement. **In parallel plot the leakage↔violation-volume Pareto front for every policy** — the lexicographic rule yields one number; the front is the scientific answer to sub-question 2. Safety threshold derived from the best baseline in Step 2, **not chosen arbitrarily**, and that derivation reported.

**Excluded: CO₂** — collinear with leakage via a fixed 176.7 kgCO₂/ML factor, and that factor is UK-specific (H7).

**Hour-resolved reporting mandatory** — closes F5; Negm located a 3–6 am vulnerability.

**DECISION: NOT LOCKED — READY TO LOCK (N1/N2/N3/N4).**

## 23. Draft Methodology Specification

> **Tagging rule strictly applied. Nothing carries `[LOCKED]`, because no researcher decision and no advisor approval is on record.** Everything is `[RECOMMENDATION — NOT LOCKED]` or `[UNRESOLVED]`.

**1. Problem formulation** — `[RECOMMENDATION — NOT LOCKED]` A **POMDP** solved as an MDP over approximated states (the agent observes neither future demand nor all nodes). Horizon 24 h; decision interval 1 h (consistent with Belfadil, Negm and Hu); episode = 24 steps; terminal at horizon end. Dynamics: each step EPANET performs a steady-state solve at the hour's demand with applied settings; tank level carries forward by volume balance — Negm's "EPS redefined as a chain of steady-state solves". `[RECOMMENDATION — NOT LOCKED]` **Declared limitation:** no transient/water-hammer dynamics, so cyclic-fatigue reduction is not directly provable; only proxies are measured. `[UNRESOLVED — A4, advisor]`

**2. Hydraulic simulation** — `[RECOMMENDATION — NOT LOCKED]` EPANET **2.2** (native Wagner PDA); WNTR ≥1.0 for network construction and scenario generation; **EpanetSimulator** for execution (mandatory — WNTRSimulator ignores emitter coefficients). **Declared limitation:** PDA parameters are necessarily **global** under EpanetSimulator. Demand model **PDA both in training and evaluation**; DDA retained as controlled ablation A7. `P₀ = 0`, `1/e = 0.5`. Mandatory pre-training gate V1–V5. `[UNRESOLVED — B4]` `P_f`, `p^min_service`, `p^max`; protocol recommendation `p^min = 20 m` reference with mandatory sensitivity S3 over {10, 14, 20, 25} and `P_f` set slightly above `p^min`. `[RECOMMENDATION — NOT LOCKED]` EPANET 2.3 / native FAVAD → future work.

**3. Network** — `[UNRESOLVED — D1, advisor]` Recommendation: **EPANET Net3** (92 nodes, 117 pipes, 2 raw sources, 2 pump stations, 3 elevated tanks; North Marin Water District; Kentucky Hydraulic Model Database). `[UNRESOLVED — E1, advisor]` PRV placement; recommendation: two sets — **P-GA** (four PRVs via GA pre-experiment on leakage impact, replicating Hu, carrying the main results) and **P-OP** (four PRVs at operationally motivated locations chosen without reference to the leakage objective, carrying a full primary-metrics reproduction as sensitivity S9). `[UNRESOLVED — D2]` Secondary network; recommendation Jowitt & Xu for a PRV-only sub-experiment, execute-decision in month 6. `[RECOMMENDATION — NOT LOCKED]` The final `.inp`, recording every modification, version-controlled in git.

**4. Leakage model** — `[RECOMMENDATION — NOT LOCKED]` `Q^leak_j = k_j · p_j^{1.18}`, `k_j ∝ Σ_i L_ij`, `k_j < 0.196 Ls⁻¹m⁻⁰·⁵` (background regime). **Mandatory calibration:** scale `k_j` so total leakage in the reference scenario equals **10 % and 20 %** of total demand (two experimental levels). WNTR-native leakage **rejected** (α locked at 0.5). Pipe-level model retained as a sensitivity. Mandatory sensitivity S1 over `N₁ ∈ {0.5, 1.0, 1.18, 1.2, 1.4}`, hard ceiling **1.5**.

**5. Demand model** — `[RECOMMENDATION — NOT LOCKED]` PDA (Wagner): `d_{j,t} = 0` for `p ≤ P₀`; `D_{j,t}((p−P₀)/(P_f−P₀))^{1/e}` for `P₀ < p < P_f`; `D_{j,t}` for `p ≥ P_f`. `DSR = Σ_{t,j} d_{j,t} / Σ_{t,j} D_{j,t}`. **Leakage flows via the emitter path, consumer demand via the PDA function — two separate paths**, which is what makes leakage and service shortfall separable. `[UNRESOLVED — G2]` exact numerical PDA↔emitter interaction, resolved by test V4.

**6. State** — `[RECOMMENDATION — NOT LOCKED]` `o_t = [p^M_t, q^F_t, h^tank_t, a_{t-1}, sin(2πt/24), cos(2πt/24)]`. Selection rule for `M`: global critical node + immediate downstream node of each PRV + one representative per pressure zone. **Two hard prohibitions:** nodal `Q^leak` never in the main observation (a model quantity, not a measurement ⇒ non-deployable policy); the **true demand multiplier never** in the observation (future-information leakage ⇒ sub-question 1 vacuous). Permitted: the *effect* of demand. Normalisation statistics from **training only**, stored and published. S3 restricted to one oracle run; S1 in ablation A8. `[UNRESOLVED — F2]` numeric sensor list, fixed after Step 0.

**7. Action** — `[RECOMMENDATION — NOT LOCKED]` `s^PRV_{v,t} = clip(s̃_{v,t}, s^PRV_{v,t-1} ± δ_v)`, `ω_{u,t} = clip(ω̃_{u,t}, ω_{u,t-1} ± δ_u)`; `s^PRV_v ∈ [p^min_service, s̄_v]` (target outlet head, metres), `ω_u ∈ [0.7, 1.0]` (mechanical constraint, Hu); `s̄_v` from **1,000 random rollouts** (Hu's empirical method). Policy outputs `tanh` rescaled to physical range ⇒ invalid actions structurally impossible. **ARR** logged: realised setting read back from EPANET each step; reported per actuator and aggregated. Pure incremental in ablation A11. `[UNRESOLVED — G2 sensitivity]` `δ` at 10 % reference, S8 optional.

**8. Reward** — `[RECOMMENDATION — NOT LOCKED]` `r_t = −[w_L L̃_t + w_V Ṽ_t + w_S S̃_t + w_E Ẽ_t]`, all terms dimensionless and globally normalised against a reference scenario; `Ṽ_t = (1/|J|)Σ_j(ν_{j,t}/ν^scale)^β` with `ν_{j,t} = max(0, p^min − p_{j,t}) + max(0, p_{j,t} − p^max)` **in metres**; `Ẽ_t` with `η = 0.75`, **no tariff modelling**; hard constraint `H_tank,fin ≥ H_tank,ini`. Mandatory pre-training battery T1, T2, T3, T4, T6, T7, T9, T10 — **T3 and T7 are hard gates**. `[UNRESOLVED — H2]` `β`: reference 2, determined by mandatory ablation A6 over {binary, 1, 2}. `[UNRESOLVED — H5]` **final weights explicitly deferred**: sweep `w_V/w_L ∈ {1/7, 1/5, 1/3, 1, 3, 5, 7}` at identical budget and seeds, report the full Pareto front, then select by feasibility-first. `[UNRESOLVED — H3]` constrained formulation, Tier 3, execute-decision in month 5. `[RECOMMENDATION — NOT LOCKED]` safety filter → future work.

**9. PPO** — `[RECOMMENDATION — NOT LOCKED]` PPO retained unchanged as the approved primary algorithm. Starting configuration `n_steps = 2048`, `batch_size = 64`, `n_epochs = 10`, `γ = 0.99`, `lr = 3e-4`, `clip = 0.2` (SB3 defaults, matching Negm's documented setup), with a declared equal tuning budget. **Justification carries a regime caveat:** the on-policy advantage has evidence only in the dynamic regime; in the quasi-static regime the opposite holds. `[UNRESOLVED — I4, advisor]` removal of the "on-policy ⇒ smaller sim-to-real gap" non-sequitur. **MADDPG / multi-agent excluded from the primary methodology.**

**10. Comparator** — `[RECOMMENDATION — NOT LOCKED]` **SAC** as the single learning comparator at equal timestep budget, equal seed count and equal tuning trials. `[UNRESOLVED — I3]` Recurrent PPO as an architectural ablation, Tier 3.

**11. Training** — `[RECOMMENDATION — NOT LOCKED]` **1–2 M timesteps** per (algorithm × weight × seed) ⇒ ≥500 policy updates. Fixed budget, **no test-based early stopping**; separate validation set for checkpoint and weight selection; both final and best checkpoints logged; learning curves reported as mean ± SD across seeds. **The four cost quantities reported separately and never conflated:** (A) training wall-clock, (B) inference/decision time, (C) environment interactions, (D) hydraulic-solver evaluations. `[UNRESOLVED — J2]` seeds: 5 recommended with conditional escalation to 10. `[UNRESOLVED — J3]` sweep cost reduction: reduced-budget sweep then full budget for the chosen weight plus one adjacent ratio, reduction declared.

**12. Demand uncertainty** — `[RECOMMENDATION — NOT LOCKED]` Two-step truncated-normal multipliers (hourly × nodal) on `(1−Δ, 1+Δ)`; large Net3 consumers excluded from randomisation; initial tank level `U(0,1)`. Train `Δ ∈ {0.3, 0.6}`; **`Δ = 0.9` fully held out for OOD testing**; out-of-phase demand pattern as a second OOD test; ≥100 test episodes per seed. Step-2 feasibility check on `Δ = 0.9`. Historical/SCADA profiles and full Monte Carlo **excluded**. Scalar perturbation optional as a cheap stress test.

**13. Evaluation** — `[RECOMMENDATION — NOT LOCKED]` Five primary metrics (leakage volume absolute and relative; violation volume in metre·hours; violation count; maximum violation; DSR); eight secondary (mean pressure, pressure variability, energy kWh, actuator movement, tank recovery, ARR, inference time, training time); learning diagnostics as listed in §17. **CO₂ excluded** (collinear with leakage). **Hour-resolved reporting mandatory.** `[RECOMMENDATION — NOT LOCKED, PRE-REGISTRATION REQUIRED]` feasibility-first lexicographic ranking with the safety threshold derived from the best baseline in Step 2, plus the leakage↔violation Pareto front reported in parallel.

**14. Baselines** — `[RECOMMENDATION — NOT LOCKED]` **Mandatory:** fixed-outlet PRV (tuned by explicit industrial criterion), TMPC, DE (documented hydraulic budget raised to plateau), single-objective PPO, SAC. **Recommended:** P-controller on the critical node, GA. **Optional:** PSO, Nelder-Mead. **Rejected:** MPC, MADDPG. Uniform fairness protocol: same network, scenarios, seeds, simulator, leakage model, constraints and locked test set; break-even ≈ 4 operational cases reported.

**15. Ablation** — `[RECOMMENDATION — NOT LOCKED]` **Tier 1:** A14, A5, A12, A7, **A6**. **Tier 2:** A8, A9, A13, A11, A1–A4 (A2's number reported explicitly as the reward-hacking upper bound). **Tier 3:** A10, constrained arm. Fairness rule: identical budget, seeds and test set across all tiers.

**16. Sensitivity** — `[RECOMMENDATION — NOT LOCKED]` **Mandatory:** S1 (`N₁`), S2 (leakage level), S3 (`p^min`), S6 (weight ratio), **S9 (PRV placement)**. Covered elsewhere: S5 (by V1–V3), S7 (by A12), S10 (by the tuning budget). Optional: S4, S8. Method: one-factor-at-a-time at 3 seeds (declared reduction), reported as a tornado plot.

**17. Statistics** — `[RECOMMENDATION — NOT LOCKED]` **Minimum defensible:** unit of replication = training seed; ≥5 seeds × ≥100 unseen test episodes; two-stage aggregation; mean ± SD + 95 % bootstrap CI; box plots per method; Mann–Whitney U; **Cliff's delta effect size leading the interpretation, p-values supporting**; Holm–Bonferroni for multiple method comparisons; all seeds reported including diverged ones. **Ideal:** 10 seeds, 200 test episodes, pre-registered analysis plan, paired tests on common scenario seeds. **Honesty rule:** where CIs overlap, state that the difference is not detectable.

**18. Reproducibility** — `[RECOMMENDATION — NOT LOCKED]` Full traceability chain and run-directory contents per §19; experiment ID scheme; three separate seed streams with the test stream never used in training; exact version pins plus `pip freeze`; hardware recorded; historical results never overwritten; modified `.inp` version-controlled. `[UNRESOLVED — Q1]` Python version; recommendation **3.12** in a dedicated venv.

## 24. Methodology Consistency Audit

| # | Potential contradiction | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **C-1** | PDA declared but DDA-only assumptions retained | ✅ **Clean.** PDA is specified for both phases; DDA appears only as ablation A7 with its own simulator configuration. Tests V1–V3 exist precisely to catch a silent fallback to DDA via the 0.07 m default |
| **C-2** | **Leakage metric without a leakage model** | 🔴 **REAL CONTRADICTION — but in the inherited documents, not in this specification.** The **Proposal** makes leakage reduction its primary objective while specifying no leakage model (`emitter`, `FAVAD`, `N₁`, `leakage exponent` all zero occurrences). §23 item 4 resolves it. **This is why the Proposal cannot be implemented as written, and it is a completion rather than a scope change.** Flagged in §22 |
| **C-3** | Future demand inside the state | ✅ **Clean, and structurally prohibited.** F4 bans the true demand multiplier explicitly; only its *effect* (observed pressures and flows) is admitted |
| **C-4** | Violation threshold inconsistent with PDA | 🟡 **TENSION — identified and mitigated, must be declared.** If `P_f` equals `p^min`, DSR and violation count become structurally correlated and are not independent metrics. Mitigation: set `P_f` slightly above `p^min`; declare the residual correlation in the interpretation. **Not resolved by construction — resolved by declaration** |
| **C-5** | Reward objective inconsistent with evaluation metric | ✅ **Clean, and deliberately aligned.** Reward terms `L̃, Ṽ, S̃, Ẽ` map onto primary metrics leakage volume and violation volume and secondary metrics actuator movement and energy. **One deliberate asymmetry:** DSR and maximum violation are evaluated but not rewarded — intentional, so that reward hacking is *detectable* by a metric the agent is not optimising. This is a feature; it is recorded so it is not mistaken for an inconsistency |
| **C-6** | PRV action range inconsistent with physics | ✅ **Clean.** Upper bound derived empirically from 1,000 rollouts rather than assumed; VSP bounded at `[0.7, 1.0]` on mechanical grounds; rate-limit projection guarantees inter-step feasibility; `tanh` rescaling makes out-of-range actions impossible. **Residual physical gap acknowledged:** the three-state PRV means a valid command may still be unrealised — which is exactly what ARR measures rather than assumes away |
| **C-7** | Baseline using a different simulator | ✅ **Clean.** M3 requires identical simulator, network, leakage model, PDA parameters, constraints, scenarios and locked test set for every baseline |
| **C-8** | Demand uncertainty in training but not testing | ✅ **Clean, and stronger than the prior work.** Uncertainty is present in train, validation and test, with `Δ = 0.9` **held out** — an advance on both Hu papers, which tested in-distribution only |
| **C-9** | Generalisation claimed without cross-network testing | ✅ **Clean by construction.** L3 is explicitly excluded and recorded as future work; L4 restricts the claim to "unseen demand scenarios and operating conditions, on the same network", with topology listed in the limitations chapter |
| **C-10** | "Real-time" claimed without decision-time measurement | ✅ **Clean, with a scale caveat.** Inference time is a secondary metric; M3 mandates the four separate cost figures. **Additional requirement:** every real-time claim must state the scale — Negm's own evidence shows <0.4 s at DMA level versus ~10 s whole-system, and Net3 at 92 nodes sits in the first regime |
| **C-11** | Energy metric without a pump model | ✅ **Clean.** The energy term uses `η = 0.75` (Hu's documented simplification) with EPANET's pump curves supplying head and flow. **Declared simplification:** constant rather than curve-derived efficiency; tariff modelling deliberately omitted on Hu's evidence that solutions track demand pattern, not tariff |
| **C-12** | Smoothness metric without previous action | ✅ **Clean.** `a_{t-1}` is in the S2 observation, which is what makes `S̃_t` computable — a dependency the state design was specified to satisfy |
| **C-13** (added) | Attribution confound: reward redesign vs tuning vs budget | 🟡 **TENSION, mitigated by design.** Negm's reward-hacking outcome is entangled across three causes. Mitigation: A6 at equal tuning and budget isolates the reward's share. **Unresolved unless A6 actually runs** — which is why it was promoted to Tier 1 |
| **C-14** (added) | Placement co-optimised with the measured objective | 🟡 **TENSION, mitigated by design.** P-GA carries the same optimistic bias Negm diagnosed. Mitigation: dual placement sets plus mandatory sensitivity S9 plus an explicit statement that leakage-reduction percentage is siting-conditional |

**Audit result: one real contradiction (C-2, inherited from the Proposal and resolved by this specification) and three tensions (C-4, C-13, C-14) that are managed by design and declaration rather than eliminated.** No internal contradiction was found within the specification of §23 itself.

## Bibliographic Record

**Title:** "Physics-Informed Safe Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning with Uncertainty-Aware Zero-shot Deployment" "for Variable-speed Heat-pump Building Control"

**Authors:**
1. Yaran Wang (first author)
2. Mohsin Khan
3. Shamsul Haq

**Affiliations:** None — the affiliation fields for all three authors are empty in this record.

**Publication year:** 2026 (posted, issued, and published all give 2026; created/deposited 24 July 2026, indexed 24 July 2026)

**Journal / venue:** No journal container is listed. This is a preprint ("posted-content," subtype "preprint") in the SSRN group, with publisher listed as Elsevier BV (Crossref member 78). Source: Crossref.

**DOI:** 10.2139/ssrn.7163762 — resolves via https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7163762; primary resource: https://www.ssrn.com/abstract=7163762

**Subject / keywords:** None supplied (the subject array is empty).

**Other metadata:** reference-count 0; is-referenced-by-count 0.

## Abstract (summarized)

The paper addresses control of electrified building heating, arguing that rule-based, optimization-based, and reinforcement-learning controllers typically need building-specific calibration, generalize poorly to new buildings, and offer no explicit safety guarantees. The authors propose a physics-informed, safe multi-agent reinforcement-learning framework for buildings served by variable-speed air-to-water heat pumps, designed for "uncertainty-aware zero-shot deployment." It couples a nonlinear physical model (multi-node building thermal dynamics, hydronic heat transfer, heat-pump performance variation, frost/defrost behavior, auxiliary heating, grid interaction) with a building-parameter-conditioned recurrent world model that embeds physical consistency and uncertainty estimation in multi-step prediction, allowing policy learning without target-building data. A centralized-training/decentralized-execution multi-agent controller coordinates heat-pump modulation, circulation-pump operation, and auxiliary heating, while a safety layer applies constraint tightening, out-of-distribution detection, action projection, and fallback control. Evaluation covers unseen heterogeneous buildings, cold-humid frosting conditions, price and carbon-intensity variation, and extreme weather. Reported results: prediction errors held "below approximately 5%" for key thermal and heat-pump variables; versus rule-based operation, seasonal cost and carbon emissions fall 21.0% and 19.0%; seasonal COP rises to 3.52; thermal comfort satisfaction 98.67%; safety violations 0.42%.

## Relevance to water distribution networks

**No.** This work does not concern water distribution networks. The only water-related element is the hydronic (air-to-water) heating circuit inside buildings — heat-pump loops, circulation pumps, and heat transfer to indoor zones. There is nothing in the record about municipal or potable water supply systems, pipe networks, leak detection, pressure management, or water demand.

## Abstract (reconstructed and summarized)

The paper's abstract argues that a central difficulty in developing leakage detection and isolation algorithms for drinking water distribution systems is benchmarking — i.e., evaluating and comparing methodologies on common problems. To address this, the "Battle of the Leakage Detection and Isolation Methods (BattLeDIM)" competition was run in 2020, intended to "objectively compare the performance of methods for the detection and localization of leakage events." Competing approaches worked from SCADA (supervisory control and data acquisition) readings of flow and pressure sensors placed in "a virtual water distribution system." Entries came from both academic and industry teams and applied a range of techniques — time series analysis, statistical methods, machine learning, mathematical programming, metaheuristics, and engineering judgment — and were scored against "realistic economic criteria." The paper reports the competition outcomes and analyzes the differing methods the teams used. Its stated conclusion is that further work on leakage detection and isolation methods is needed, along with "additional open benchmark problems" for that purpose.

## Reconstructed abstract (paraphrased in detail; short quotes only)

**Pei, S., Hoang, L., Fu, G., & Butler, D. (2025). "Real-Time Pump Scheduling in Water Distribution Networks Using Deep Reinforcement Learning." *Journal of Water Resources Planning and Management* (ASCE). DOI: 10.1061/JWRMD5.WRENG-6476. Not open access.**

The paper opens by noting that how pumps are scheduled in water distribution networks (WDNs) affects both energy efficiency and reliability of supply. Conventional optimisation approaches, the authors argue, run into two recurring obstacles: heavy computational demands and difficulty coping with uncertain water demand.

Their proposed remedy is a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approach based on proximal policy optimization (PPO) for "real-time pump scheduling in WDNs." Because PPO agents are trained beforehand to yield offline policies, the online optimisation step that would otherwise be executed throughout the scheduling horizon is eliminated.

Evaluation is against genetic-algorithm–based baselines on two networks. Reported findings:

- The PPO agents beat the robust optimisation baseline on operational cost and on "robustness to demand uncertainty."
- They match the online optimisation baselines in scheduling performance.
- Feeding demand and time information into the agent's inputs during training raises DRL performance.
- Reducing the scheduling step size can further improve the agents.

The conclusion frames the work as demonstrating PPO's promise for real-time pump scheduling and offering guidance for developing and applying the method in practice.

**Network details not present.** The repository page provides no information about the L-Town network topology — no counts of nodes, pipes, pumps, tanks, reservoirs, PRVs/valves, or DMAs/pressure zones. It also does not state how many leaks are in the dataset, what SCADA signals (flow/pressure) are recorded at which sensors, the sampling interval, or the dataset's start/end dates. Those specifics would have to come from the linked website ([battledim.ucy.ac.cy](https://battledim.ucy.ac.cy/)) or the journal paper.

The only related statement is a general description of the challenge: comparing leak detection and localization methods "relying on SCADA measurements of flow and pressure sensors installed within water distribution networks." The results-template examples use 2019 timestamps (e.g. `p23, 2019-05-19 02:05`), which hints the evaluation year is 2019, but the page does not confirm the dataset period.

The README does state a dependency: the work "uses the EPANET-Matlab-Toolkit which is a Matlab class for EPANET libraries," implying an EPANET model is used by the generator scripts.

## Abstract (reconstructed from the inverted index, summarised)

The inverted index resolves into a continuous 193-token abstract. Its content, in my own words:

Shortages of both energy and water make the joint management of these resources in water distribution networks (WDNs) ever more pressing, yet scheduling pumps and valves live in changing conditions is still hard. The authors therefore put forward a multi-agent reinforcement-learning scheduling framework aimed at handling uncertain water demand. Their steps: build a WDN environment and cast scheduling as a Markov decision process; apply MADDPG to derive a policy for what they describe as a "fully cooperative multi-agent task"; examine how energy and water-loss costs shape that policy; then benchmark against GA, PSO and DE for performance and robustness. Findings: "water loss dominates the scheduling process", the cost-minimising schedules track "the demand pattern of consumers rather than the energy tariff", and MADDPG beats the three baselines while reaching a "significantly faster solution", useful in practice.

(Quoted fragments are verbatim; the surrounding narrative is a paraphrase rather than a full word-for-word transcription.)

## Elements asked about

- **Network:** water distribution networks (WDNs) — a WDN environment was built for training/evaluation; no specific benchmark network name is given in this record.
- **Actuators:** pumps and valves, scheduled in real time.
- **Algorithm:** multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient (MADDPG), framed as a cooperative multi-agent Markov decision process; compared with genetic algorithm (GA), particle swarm optimisation (PSO) and differential evolution (DE).
- **Demand model:** uncertain / dynamic water demand, characterised through consumer demand patterns, which the results identify as the dominant driver of scheduling solutions (over the energy tariff).

## Record summary

**Title:** "Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning for Water Management"

**Authors:** Zuzanna Osika; Roxana Rădulescu; Jazmin Zatarain-Salazar; Frans A. Oliehoek; Pradeep K. Murukannaiah

**Year:** 2025 (published/issued 28 May 2025; deposited to Crossref January 2026)

**Venue:** Listed under the container title "International Joint Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems" (AAMAS), pp. 2702–2704 — a short paper / extended-abstract length entry. Note that the metadata is internally inconsistent: the `event` field names the *Third* AAMAS ("AAMAS '04", New York), while the publisher field says IEEE Computer Society and the primary resource URL points to an ACM Digital Library record (10.5555/3709347.3743984). DOI: 10.65109/zjze7221; ISSN 1558-2914.

**Abstract (paraphrased):** Many practical problems — the authors cite resource management, autonomous driving and drug discovery — involve trading off objectives that conflict. Multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) generalises standard RL so that several objectives are treated at once, producing a family of policies spanning different trade-offs. The authors argue the field "lacks complex, realistic environments and benchmarks," and respond by casting a water-resource case study as a MORL environment, then evaluating existing MORL algorithms on it. Their finding is that domain-specific water management techniques do better than current MORL methods, which "underscor[es] the scalability challenges MORL algorithms face in real-world scenarios."

## Is this about water *distribution networks*?

**No.** This is river-basin / reservoir water-resource management, not pressurised drinking-water distribution networks (pipes, pumps, valves, tanks, leakage, water quality).

- **System studied:** the Nile river basin, described as a "water resource (Nile river basin) management case study" modelled as a MORL environment.
- **What is controlled:** the record does not say. The abstract only states the case study is modelled as a MORL environment; it names no action space (basin-scale work of this type typically concerns reservoir release/operating decisions, but that is inference, not stated here).
- **Algorithm:** none singled out. The contribution is a benchmark — the authors "benchmark existing MORL algorithms on this task" and compare against "specialized water management methods." No specific algorithm names appear in this metadata.
- **Objectives:** not enumerated. Only the general claim of multiple conflicting objectives is given; the individual objectives are not listed in the available record.

The full paper would be needed for the action space, the specific algorithms compared, and the objective definitions.

## What the page actually states about L-Town

**Network character:** L-Town is described as "a small hypothetical town which experiences a large number of pipe breaks and water losses," affecting service quality. The model and data were derived from a real water distribution network in a Cypriot city — i.e., it is a realistic but synthetic benchmark rather than a literal utility model.

**Component-level detail is not available in this source.** The page gives no counts for junctions/nodes, pipes, pumps, tanks, reservoirs, isolation valves or pressure-reducing valves, and it does not state the number of pressure zones or DMAs. It also does not state how many leak events occurred, only that there were many. Any specific figures I offered would be invention, not extraction.

**Sensors and data period (partial):** Participants worked from "SCADA measurements of flow and pressure sensors installed within water distribution networks." Two datasets were supplied: a historical year, 2018, and an evaluation year, 2019, with the task being to detect and localize leaks occurring in 2019. Sensor counts, tag names, sampling interval and units are not given here. Release milestones: the 2018 data appeared 27/12/2019, a revised network plus 2018 data on 20/1/2020, and the 2019 evaluation data on 24/1/2020.

**EPANET model:** The text confirms an "L-Town EPANET model" was created and distributed, but no `.inp` filename, version or download path is specified on this page.

| Resource | Location |
|---|---|
| BattLeDIM dataset (Zenodo archive) | `https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.4017658` |
| Evaluation code | `https://github.com/KIOS-Research/BattLeDIM` (KIOS-Research) |
| Runnable evaluation capsule | `https://codeocean.com/capsule/2366240` |
| Workshop presentations | `https://zenodo.org/record/4139603` |

| Overview paper | `https://doi.org/10.1061/(ASCE)WR.1943-5452.0001601` |

Site sections that likely hold the missing specifics are "Dataset" (`?page_id=33`), its "Results Template" subpage (`?page_id=144`), "Challenge" (`?page_id=30`) and "FAQ" (`?page_id=95`).

## Where to get the hydraulic inventory

The Rules PDF and the Zenodo record are the two places the topology, element counts, DMA structure, sensor inventory and leak ground truth would be documented; the Zenodo deposit is also where the EPANET input file would reside. Note that GitHub and Zenodo materials carry their own license terms, which should be checked before reuse.

The battle was originally arranged for the 2nd International CCWI/WDSA Joint Conference in Beijing, which COVID-19 forced to be cancelled; an online pre-conference workshop ran 3/9/2020 instead, with special-collection papers due by 30/04/2021.

content.content:
## Reconstructed abstract (paraphrased, with short verbatim fragments in quotes)

**Highlights (5 bullet points), in substance:** the authors report building a DRL framework that couples forecasting with "automated control"; improved water-quality prediction versus benchmark approaches; capture of "time-varying reaction coefficients through dynamic calibration"; effective identification, isolation and flushing of contamination events; and gains in both modelling skill and response efficiency in water distribution systems (WDSs).

**Main abstract, in substance:** Drinking water reaches consumers via "complex water-distribution systems (WDSs)," typical of virtually all urbanised areas. Contaminants may linger and travel through such networks because of inadequate disinfection at treatment plants or ingress from outside, so both accurate forecasting of contaminant transport and automated mitigation are described as "critical." The paper therefore presents "deep reinforcement learning (DRL)-based models to enhance water-quality management in WDSs."

The first model couples EPANET 2.2 (US Environmental Protection Agency Network Evaluation Tool) simulations with "real-time sensor data to optimize reaction coefficients." It beat both benchmarks at all six sensors over the validation period, with mean R² gains of 20.9% and 21.2% and RMSE cuts of 11.3% and 21.7% against the "ensemble Kalman filter and pattern-search method," respectively. "Performance gains were most pronounced at terminal nodes, where water stagnates" and reaction coefficients matter more than in high-circulation zones.

The second model uses a "double deep Q-network to automatically operate valves and hydrants upon contaminant detection," reaching an "average 90.7% contaminant removal within 5 h across 100 simulated incidents."

The conclusion: the automated system located and isolated contaminated areas effectively, showing that a DRL-based framework can improve "both predictive modeling and operational responsiveness," and stressing the value of data assimilation plus autonomous control in modern water-quality management.

## Answers to your specific questions

| Question | Answer from this record |
|---|---|
| Network used and size | **Not stated.** No case-study network name or node/pipe count appears; the only scale indicator is six water-quality sensors and 100 simulated contamination scenarios. EPANET 2.2 is the simulator. |
| What is controlled | **Valves and hydrants** (i.e., isolation plus flushing). No mention of PRVs or pumps. |
| Algorithm | Deep reinforcement learning; the control agent is a **double deep Q-network (DDQN)**. A second DRL model performs dynamic calibration/data assimilation of reaction coefficients, benchmarked against an ensemble Kalman filter and a pattern-search method. |
| Leakage or pressure objective? | **Neither.** Objectives are water-quality: prediction accuracy (R², RMSE) and contaminant removal fraction/time. |
| Demand model | **Not specified** in this record (no demand pattern, stochastic or otherwise, is described). |
| Uncertainty / generalisation evaluated? | **Partially.** Testing spans 100 simulated incidents and a separate validation period across six sensors, and the calibration baseline (EnKF) is uncertainty-oriented; however no formal uncertainty quantification, sensitivity analysis, or transfer to a different network is reported here. |

Caveat: this is derived solely from the OpenAlex metadata/inverted-index abstract, so details confined to the full text (network topology, demand modelling, hyperparameters) cannot be confirmed.

# فاز جدید: بازبینی مستقل و عمیق انتخاب شبکه، طراحی آزمایش و نوآوری پایان‌نامه

## نقش تو

تو در این فاز صرفاً «دستیار کدنویسی» یا «تأییدکننده‌ی تصمیم‌های قبلی» نیستی.

نقش تو یک **پژوهشگر ارشد، داور سخت‌گیر PhD/Master، و مهندس WDN + DRL** است که باید انتخاب‌های فعلی پایان‌نامه را به‌صورت **adversarial** بررسی کند.

هیچ‌کدام از تصمیم‌های قبلی را فقط به دلیل اینکه در Phase 1/2/3 پیشنهاد شده‌اند، درست فرض نکن.

به‌خصوص درباره‌ی **انتخاب شبکه** از نتیجه‌گیری قبلی دفاع نکن و از Net3 به‌صورت پیش‌فرض حمایت نکن.

هدف این فاز این است که قبل از نوشتن کد و اجرای آزمایش، یک بار دیگر مشخص شود:

1. بهترین شبکه برای پایان‌نامه واقعاً کدام است؟
2. آیا می‌توان از همان شبکه‌ی Negm به‌عنوان پایه استفاده کرد و اجزای جدید مثل پمپ و PRV اضافه کرد؟
3. آیا چنین تغییری علمی و قابل‌دفاع است یا benchmark را خراب می‌کند؟
4. آیا Net3 واقعاً بهترین انتخاب است یا شبکه‌ی عمومی دیگری بهتر است؟
5. اگر قرار باشد شبکه‌ای را اصلاح کنیم، دقیقاً چه اصلاحاتی مجاز و قابل‌دفاع‌اند؟
6. این انتخاب چه اثری بر RQ، novelty، fairness، reproducibility، computation و طراحی آزمایش دارد؟
7. در نهایت، **یک تصمیم روشن و قابل اجرا** بده که بتوانم بر اساس آن وارد implementation شوم.

---

# CONTEXT پروژه

پایان‌نامه درباره‌ی کنترل فشار در Water Distribution Network با استفاده از Deep Reinforcement Learning است.

هسته‌ی روش:

* EPANET
* WNTR
* PPO
* continuous action space
* PRV control
* Variable-Speed Pump (VSP)
* leakage minimization
* pressure/service constraints
* stochastic demand
* uncertainty/generalization
* multi-objective reward
* مقایسه با baselineهای کلاسیک و RL

Research Question اصلی تقریباً حول این ایده است:

> آیا PPO می‌تواند با کنترل هماهنگ PRV و پمپ، در شرایط تقاضای متغیر و نامطمئن، فشار را تنظیم کرده و leakage را کاهش دهد، بدون اینکه کیفیت سرویس/pressure constraints به شکل غیرقابل‌قبول نقض شوند؟

Proposal چند innovation دارد، اما بعد از مرور ادبیات مشخص شده که بسیاری از ادعاهای اولیه novelty بیش از حد بوده‌اند.

بنابراین novelty نباید با ادعاهای زیر تعریف شود:

* continuous action برای اولین بار
* EPANET + PPO برای اولین بار
* PRV + pump coordination برای اولین بار
* multi-objective reward برای اولین بار

چون شواهدی علیه این ادعاها پیدا شده است.

به‌جای آن، نوآوری احتمالی بیشتر در **طراحی آزمایش، attribution، observability، PDA/DDA، uncertainty separation، Pareto evaluation و robustness analysis** قرار دارد.

---

# PRIOR WORK مهم

## Negm 2024

کار بسیار نزدیک به پروژه است.

در Jowitt & Xu:

* 25 junction
* 37 pipe
* 3 valves
* 0 pumps
* 3 tanks/reservoirs
* 1 DMA

Negm از DRL برای pressure/leakage control استفاده کرده است.

PPO، Recurrent PPO و الگوریتم‌های دیگر را بررسی کرده است.

در نتایج معروف:

* PPO حدود 73.4% water saving نشان داده
* ولی حدود 304 pressure violations داشته
* DE حدود 65.9% water saving و فقط 46 violations داشته

Negm همچنین در بخش future work پیشنهاد اضافه‌کردن pressure-influencing elements مانند pumps را مطرح می‌کند.

نکته‌ی بسیار مهم:

Jowitt & Xu **پمپ ندارد**.

بنابراین شبکه‌ی اصلی Negm برای یک پایان‌نامه که innovation اصلی آن coordinated PRV + VSP است، به‌طور مستقیم مناسب نیست.

---

# Hu et al. 2023

Hu روی Net3 کار کرده است.

Net3 شامل تقریباً:

* 92 nodes
* 117 pipes
* 2 pump stations
* 3 elevated tanks
* 2 raw water sources

و برای pump + valve control استفاده شده است.

Hu برای این شبکه PRV اضافه کرده و از RL/optimization برای کنترل استفاده کرده است.

بنابراین Net3 از نظر ساختار، بسیار مناسب مسئله‌ی ماست.

اما باید توجه کنی که:

**Net3 دیگر یک مسئله‌ی کاملاً جدید نیست.**

کارهای قبلی روی Net3 انجام شده‌اند.

---

# مسئله‌ای که باید از نو بررسی کنی

ما تا اینجا بیش از حد روی دو شبکه متمرکز شده‌ایم:

1. Jowitt & Xu
2. Net3

اما واقعیت این است که شبکه‌های بسیار بیشتری وجود دارند.

شبکه‌هایی مانند:

* Jowitt & Xu
* Net3
* D-Town
* Anytown
* D-Town variants
* EXNET
* EX2 / Exmoor
* Ky1 / Louisville
* Hanoi / Net4
* Richmond
* Modena
* Wolf-Cordera
* WNTR example networks
* Kentucky hydraulic benchmark networks
* Exeter benchmark networks
* و هر benchmark عمومی دیگری که در منابع علمی معتبر پیدا می‌کنی

باید بررسی شوند.

**ممنوع است که فقط بین Jowitt & Xu و Net3 انتخاب کنی.**

---

# سؤال اصلی این فاز

## آیا می‌توان از شبکه‌ی Negm استفاده کرد و پمپ/شیر اضافه کرد؟

این موضوع را دقیقاً بررسی کن.

سه سناریو را از هم جدا کن:

### سناریو A

Jowitt & Xu را همان‌طور که هست استفاده کنیم.

### سناریو B

Jowitt & Xu را اصلاح کنیم:

* اضافه‌کردن pump
* اضافه‌کردن/تغییر PRV
* تعیین pump curve
* تعیین tank/source behaviour
* تعیین control rules
* تعیین pump speed range
* احتمالاً اصلاح topology

### سناریو C

یک benchmark عمومی دیگر مثل Net3 را انتخاب کنیم و تغییرات حداقلی لازم را انجام دهیم.

برای هر سناریو بررسی کن:

* آیا benchmark هنوز همان benchmark اصلی محسوب می‌شود؟
* آیا comparison با Negm حفظ می‌شود؟
* آیا comparison با literature خراب می‌شود؟
* آیا topology modification باعث می‌شود دیگر نتایج را نتوان به benchmark اصلی نسبت داد؟
* آیا modification scientifically justified است؟
* آیا این تغییرات arbitrary هستند؟
* آیا pump addition باعث ایجاد degrees of freedom جدید می‌شود؟
* آیا نتایج قابل reproducibility هستند؟
* آیا این کار novelty واقعی ایجاد می‌کند یا صرفاً یک شبکه مصنوعی جدید می‌سازد؟
* آیا یک داور می‌تواند بگوید «این دیگر Jowitt & Xu نیست»؟
* آیا fair comparison با Negm ممکن می‌ماند؟

**این سؤال را جدی بررسی کن؛ جواب سطحی نمی‌خواهم.**

---

# الزام مهم: جست‌وجوی واقعی وب

در این فاز نباید فقط از memory یا corpus فعلی استفاده کنی.

باید یک **Deep / Adversarial Literature + Benchmark Search** واقعی انجام دهی.

بازه‌ی زمانی اصلی برای novelty:

**2024–2026**

اما برای benchmark networks و کارهای پایه، منابع قدیمی‌تر هم مجازند.

حداقل این دسته‌ها را جست‌وجو کن:

### 1. Public WDN benchmarks

شبکه‌هایی که:

* EPANET-compatible باشند
* فایل مدل در دسترس باشد
* node/pipe/pump/tank/valve مشخص داشته باشند
* قابلیت reproducibility داشته باشند

### 2. WDN + DRL

جست‌وجو برای:

* reinforcement learning
* deep reinforcement learning
* PPO
* SAC
* TD3
* pump control
* PRV control
* pressure management
* leakage reduction
* demand uncertainty

### 3. Joint pump + PRV control

به‌صورت خاص:

* pump + PRV
* pump + valve coordination
* continuous control
* pressure management
* leakage reduction

### 4. Benchmark papers

به دنبال papersی باش که network را explicitly معرفی کرده‌اند و بگویند:

* چرا این شبکه انتخاب شده
* network size
* pump count
* tank count
* PRV count
* public/private بودن
* availability

### 5. جدیدترین کارهای 2024، 2025 و 2026

این بخش باید adversarial باشد.

به‌خصوص بررسی کن آیا بعد از Cyriac & Chacko 2026، مقاله‌ای آمده که:

* continuous-action pressure control
* pump + PRV
* Net3
* D-Town
* public benchmark
* uncertainty
* leakage
* PPO/SAC

را ترکیب کرده باشد.

**هیچ novelty claim را بدون search کامل قبول نکن.**

---

# قانون FACT / INFERENCE

برای تمام نتیجه‌گیری‌ها این تفکیک را رعایت کن:

### FACT

چیزی که مستقیماً از paper/database/model file قابل مشاهده است.

### INFERENCE

نتیجه‌ای که از facts استنباط می‌کنی.

هیچ inference را به شکل citation مستقیم ارائه نکن.

مثلاً:

FACT:

> Net3 دارای 92 node و 2 pump است.

INFERENCE:

> بنابراین برای controlled pump+PRV RL نسبت به Jowitt & Xu مناسب‌تر است.

این دو را از هم جدا کن.

---

# خروجی مورد انتظار

## بخش 1 — Executive Decision

در همان ابتدای گزارش بگو:

### آیا Net3 واقعاً بهترین انتخاب است؟

یکی از این چهار حکم را بده:

* YES
* PROBABLY YES
* UNCERTAIN
* NO

و دلیل را در حداکثر 1 صفحه توضیح بده.

---

# بخش 2 — Full Benchmark Landscape

حداقل **15 شبکه** را بررسی کن.

برای هر شبکه:

| Network | Nodes | Pipes | Pumps | Tanks | PRVs | Public? | EPANET? | RL precedent? | Leakage suitability | Pump+PRV suitability | Compute | Reproducibility | Notes |

اگر عددی را نمی‌توانی تأیید کنی:

**UNKNOWN**

بنویس.

هیچ عددی را حدس نزن.

---

# بخش 3 — Weighted Network Ranking

یک scoring framework بساز.

معیارها:

1. Pump availability
2. PRV availability
3. Tank dynamics
4. Leakage modelling
5. Demand uncertainty compatibility
6. Public availability
7. Reproducibility
8. RL computational feasibility
9. Existing RL precedent
10. Existing pump+PRV precedent
11. Benchmark comparability
12. Network realism
13. External validity
14. Ability to isolate pump contribution
15. Ability to study PDA vs DDA
16. PRV-placement transparency
17. availability of official .inp
18. number of researchers already using it

برای هر معیار:

0–5

و سپس یک score نهایی بساز.

اما:

**وزن معیارها را از خودت قایم نکن.**

صریحاً بگو چرا مثلاً computational feasibility وزن بیشتری از network size دارد.

---

# بخش 4 — Jowitt & Xu Modification Audit

این بخش خیلی مهم است.

سؤال:

## «آیا می‌توان Jowitt & Xu را تبدیل به شبکه‌ی اصلی کرد؟»

سه سطح modification را بررسی کن:

### Level 0

فقط استفاده از شبکه اصلی.

### Level 1

تغییر کم:

* اضافه کردن pump
* اضافه کردن PRV
* بدون تغییر اساسی topology

### Level 2

تغییر اساسی:

* pumps
* tanks
* curves
* controls
* topology
* source behaviour

برای هر سطح بگو:

* علمی؟
* reproducible؟
* comparable؟
* defensible؟
* خطر artificiality؟
* خطر novelty inflation؟
* چه چیزهایی باید فرض شوند؟

و پاسخ صریح بده:

### «آیا بعد از این modification هنوز می‌توان گفت این Jowitt & Xu benchmark است؟»

---

# بخش 5 — Jowitt & Xu vs Net3

یک مقایسه‌ی عمیق انجام بده.

نه فقط از نظر size.

از نظر:

* research question compatibility
* objective 1
* innovation 1
* innovation 2
* innovation 3
* pump-control feasibility
* PRV control
* leakage
* demand uncertainty
* tanks
* stochastic dynamics
* observation design
* action dimension
* reward design
* baseline comparability
* novelty
* external validity
* reproducibility
* computational cost
* advisor defensibility

در پایان:

**یک Winner انتخاب کن.**

---

# بخش 6 — آیا Jowitt & Xu باید اصلاً وارد Main Experiment شود؟

سه مدل پیشنهاد بده:

### Model A

Net3 فقط

### Model B

Net3 main + Jowitt & Xu secondary

### Model C

Jowitt & Xu modified main + Net3 secondary

و با معیارهای:

* scientific validity
* novelty
* fairness
* computation
* schedule
* reproducibility
* viva defensibility

امتیاز بده.

---

# بخش 7 — PRV Placement Problem

این موضوع قبلاً در Phaseهای قبلی مهم تشخیص داده شده است.

اما آن را دوباره بررسی کن.

به‌خصوص:

* PRV placement by GA
* operational placement
* pressure-zone boundary
* critical node
* leakage-based placement
* optimized placement bias

بررسی کن آیا استفاده از Hu's four-valve GA placement باعث:

**objective leakage co-optimization bias**

می‌شود یا خیر.

سه طراحی پیشنهاد بده:

1. Hu replication
2. operational placement
3. dual-placement experiment

و بگو کدام scientifically strongest است.

---

# بخش 8 — Network + PRV Placement Joint Decision

در نهایت تصمیم را مستقل از هم نگیر.

ممکن است یک شبکه خوب باشد ولی placement آن بد باشد.

بنابراین:

> network × PRV placement

را به‌صورت یک design problem مشترک ارزیابی کن.

مثلاً:

Net3 + Hu placement

در مقابل:

Net3 + operational placement

در مقابل:

J&X original

در مقابل:

J&X modified

و مشخص کن کدام ترکیب از نظر thesis strongest است.

---

# بخش 9 — Novelty Re-audit

تمام noveltyهای قبلی را دوباره بررسی کن.

برای هر ادعا بنویس:

* Claim
* Closest paper
* Year
* Exact overlap
* Remaining difference
* Novelty level
* Confidence
* Search gap

حداقل این claims:

1. PRV + VSP
2. PPO continuous action
3. multi-objective reward
4. leakage + pressure
5. demand uncertainty
6. OOD testing
7. observability constraint
8. PDA vs DDA
9. pump contribution ablation
10. Pareto front
11. Action Realization Rate
12. equal tuning budget
13. multi-seed evaluation

هیچ claim سبز یا «novel» را بدون evidence قوی اعلام نکن.

---

# بخش 10 — Red-Team Questions

خودت را جای داور بگذار و حداقل 15 سؤال سخت مطرح کن.

مثلاً:

* چرا Net3؟
* چرا Jowitt & Xu نیست؟
* چرا شبکه‌ی خودت را تغییر داده‌ای؟
* آیا بعد از اضافه کردن pump، هنوز benchmark استاندارد است؟
* چرا این PRV locations؟
* چرا چهار PRV؟
* چرا PPO؟
* چرا SAC فقط comparator است؟
* چرا DDA؟
* چرا PDA؟
* leakage reduction واقعاً saving است یا service curtailment؟
* اگر DE بهتر شد چه؟
* اگر PPO شکست خورد چه؟
* اگر cross-network generalization نداری چرا می‌گویی generalization؟
* آیا reward خودش leakage را manufacture می‌کند؟
* آیا time encoding باعث learned TMPC نشده؟
* آیا sensor subset واقعاً deployable است؟
* آیا stochastic demand واقعاً uncertainty است؟
* آیا Net3 به اندازه کافی realistic است؟
* آیا results فقط benchmark-specific هستند؟

برای هر سؤال یک پاسخ دفاعی کوتاه بنویس.

---

# بخش 11 — Final Recommendation

در نهایت فقط یکی از این ساختارها را پیشنهاد بده:

### OPTION 1

Net3 primary + Jowitt & Xu secondary

### OPTION 2

Net3 primary only

### OPTION 3

Modified Jowitt & Xu primary + Net3 secondary

### OPTION 4

یک network جدید که در search پیدا کرده‌ای

اما فقط با evidence انتخاب کن.

همچنین دقیقاً بگو:

* چرا گزینه‌های دیگر رد شدند؟
* چه چیزی scientifically lost می‌شود؟
* چه چیزی به‌دست می‌آید؟

---

# بخش 12 — Implementation Gate

در پایان، مشخص کن آیا بعد از این فاز می‌توان وارد implementation شد یا نه.

اگر NO:

دقیقاً بگو چه decisionهایی هنوز باید قفل شوند.

اگر YES:

دقیقاً configuration پیشنهادی را ارائه کن:

```text
NETWORK =
LEAKAGE MODEL =
DEMAND MODEL =
PDA/DDA =
PRV PLACEMENT =
PUMP MODEL =
STATE =
ACTION =
REWARD =
UNCERTAINTY =
PPO =
BASELINES =
TEST PROTOCOL =
SEEDS =
```

---

# قوانین سخت این فاز

1. از نتیجه قبلی درباره Net3 دفاع نکن.
2. از Jowitt & Xu هم صرفاً به خاطر اینکه Negm استفاده کرده دفاع نکن.
3. حداقل 15 network بررسی کن.
4. هرجا داده نداری UNKNOWN بنویس.
5. هیچ عددی را حدس نزن.
6. source را برای هر claim مهم مشخص کن.
7. 2024–2026 را به‌صورت adversarial جست‌وجو کن.
8. novelty را conservative ارزیابی کن.
9. «public» را با evidence تأیید کن.
10. اگر .inp در دسترس است، availability آن را بررسی کن.
11. اگر network modification لازم است، modification را دقیقاً مستند کن.
12. مشخص کن آیا modification هنوز benchmark را معتبر نگه می‌دارد.
13. distinction بین FACT و INFERENCE را در کل گزارش حفظ کن.
14. هیچ تصمیمی را به خاطر Phaseهای قبلی «locked» فرض نکن.
15. هیچ کدی ننویس.
16. هیچ dependency نصب نکن.
17. هیچ experiment اجرا نکن.
18. فقط research, evidence, decision analysis انجام بده.

---

# مهم‌ترین دستور

من نمی‌خواهم تو به من بگویی:

> «Net3 قبلاً انتخاب شده، پس همان را نگه می‌داریم.»

این پاسخ قابل قبول نیست.

می‌خواهم مستقل بررسی کنی:

> **اگر امروز، بدون هیچ تصمیم قبلی، از صفر بخواهیم یک benchmark عمومی برای پایان‌نامه‌ی PPO + PRV + VSP + leakage + demand uncertainty انتخاب کنیم، دقیقاً کدام شبکه را انتخاب می‌کنیم و چرا؟**

و سپس یک سؤال دوم:

> **آیا بهتر است Jowitt & Xu را اصلاح کنیم و پمپ/اجزای لازم را به آن اضافه کنیم، یا این کار از نظر علمی benchmark را تغییر می‌دهد و بهتر است Net3/شبکه‌ی دیگری را انتخاب کنیم؟**

اگر پاسخ واقعی این بود که Net3 بهترین نیست، صریحاً Net3 را رد کن.

اگر پاسخ واقعی این بود که modified Jowitt & Xu بهتر است، همان را پیشنهاد بده.

اگر هیچ گزینه‌ای قطعاً برتر نیست، عدم قطعیت را صریح اعلام کن و یک decision framework ارائه بده.

هدف این فاز **رسیدن به درست‌ترین تصمیم علمی است، نه تأیید تصمیم‌های قبلی.**
